Gautengs welfare in crisis

By: Anina Peens | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Is Gauteng's social welfare sector heading for a fall?

Unique Selling Point:
Private institutions in Gauteng caring for the most vulnerable face an uncertain future amid government actions that make little sense.

Summary:
Shockwaves were sent through the NGO sector when the department of social development in April announced drastic budgets cuts. The sector protested hard, and an urgent meeting was called. Local government was warned that if they continue with this plan, they will have a Life Esidimeni case on hands, of immeasurable proportions. Then they turned around and said, “Sorry, we didn’t mean it”. A misunderstanding? That’s an easy way out. When the announcement came, many NGOs closed their doors, while others immediately sold assets to pay April’ salaries.

Further information:
A LITTLE TOO LATE
When the new departmental contract arrived at NGOs on 15 May, it suddenly included a disclaimer that was never there before. It basically says, the department is only paying subsidy for the next twelve months and that they don’t have to pay it again next year, should they decide so. These decisions are based on the local office’s approval of an NGO’s operation. The contract can end if there is non-compliance to technical points, significant or insignificant it may be, to the work of the NGO. These include for example, zoning rights. If an NGO has been helping vulnerable people in a residential setup without the correct zoning, funding will be retracted and people who receive help must get it elsewhere.

A PREVAILING PROBLEM
Two years ago, we reported on the lack of facilities in the province. There are not enough orphanages, youth care centers, places of safety or shelters in Gauteng. To top that, the department doesn’t employ enough social workers to deal with the magnitude of cases the province faces. And there are already thousands of cases unattended because underfunded NGOs cannot do all the work. If they are closed down due to disappearing financial support, how will the state manage without them and where will the subsidies go?

But for now, they wait, in angst for the department’s next move that may leave them in the cold.
Although the department signed renewed contracts with NGOs, they have not seen a cent of the money. The standing arrangement was that contracts were signed in April and money was paid out during May. But the department caused its own administrative nightmare, and it doesn’t seem that it has the capacity to rectify a problem it caused for itself. This directly affects the most vulnerable in society. And while there may be many political decisions that led to this mess, Ya Bana’s owners must hustle for money to feed 50 little mouths. All extramural lessons, keeping these kids motivated, must be canceled. 46 of the children placed here, were sent by the Gauteng department of social development itself. It expects the services but does not want to pay for it.

MONEY WELL SPENT?
Amidst all the turmoil the department caused in the sector, various questions are being raised about how the department chooses to spend its money. Two weeks ago, Gauteng premier Panyaza Lesufi and the MEC of social development, Mbali Hlope announced the Cleaner Greener Gauteng project. Under Lesufi the department of social development was merged with the department of agriculture. It is not clear what the reasoning was behind the merge.
The cleaner greener project of the new combined department now employs 6000 people to clean streets and maintain community vegetable gardens. Is this a sustainable solution for poverty relief and job creation in the region at the expense of institutions like Ya Bana that is already making a massive difference? Or is politics in the light of next years’ election the real reason behind local governments’ questionable management of money allocated for vulnerable citizens?

SHORT CASE STUDY FOR REFERANCE: The West Rand center for people with disabilities sold its two most crucial assets, its seven-seater van, and its 20-seater bus. These vehicles are used by underpaid care workers who make daily trips to care for bed ridden quadruples, across the West Rand. Other NGOs closed their doors and numerous social workers were retrenched across the board.
How can a local government be so detached from the realities faced by the very people they are supposed to serve? The April announcement has resulted in tell-tale signs of the eventual collapse of the entire social welfare system.

YA BANA’S STORY
Ya Bana has still not received its renewed contract. In fact, the orphanage is still waiting for last years’ subsidy. And before that, it has been waiting since 2017 for the Tshwane metro to approve plans to build the orphanage. Despite this, the department approved and registered Ya Bana. Now, there seems to be a sudden turnaround.
In 2014, the department issued a certificate, which allowed Ya Bana to care for 30 children. In 2017, it registered the home to care for 60 kids and the department itself started to place children in Ya Bana’s care. Last year the department renewed the registration, and a contract was signed. To date, not a cent has been paid out. The disclaimer in the new contract now allows the department to negate it obligation to Ya bana, on the basis of the fact that the land is zoned for agriculture. The owners write to DSD every single day but there is no one responding on the other side. They have gone so far as to write to the deputy general director, Onkemetse Kabasia, who played a central role in the budget scandal. But to date, Ya Bana has received no response from either the department or the metro.
Meanwhile, a land grab on Ya Bana’s land is well underway. Four of the village’s eight hectares have been taken up by illegal shack dwellers. The children now share the land with loads of people from outside, compromising their safety. Government is doing nothing to stop the land grabs, but Ya Bana is told, they are illegally operating a house for vulnerable children.

Press Release:


Un-Welfare
Non-governmental organisations are the backbone of the social care system in Gauteng. They provide food, shelter, and medical care for some of the most vulnerable members of society, often reaching people and places that government simply can’t. Now, as Gauteng considers a policy shift for NGOs, which could reduce the very funding that these organisations need to keep afloat, the social security net that has been supporting those in need could finally crumble. But why is government so intent on changing the playing field?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Is Gauteng's social welfare sector heading for a fall?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Private institutions in Gauteng caring for the most vulnerable face an uncertain future amid government actions that make little sense.
metadata.Summary: Shockwaves were sent through the NGO sector when the department of social development in April announced drastic budgets cuts. The sector protested hard, and an urgent meeting was called. Local government was warned that if they continue with this plan, they will have a Life Esidimeni case on hands, of immeasurable proportions. Then they turned around and said, “Sorry, we didn’t mean it”. A misunderstanding? That’s an easy way out. When the announcement came, many NGOs closed their doors, while others immediately sold assets to pay April’ salaries.
metadata.Further information: A LITTLE TOO LATE When the new departmental contract arrived at NGOs on 15 May, it suddenly included a disclaimer that was never there before. It basically says, the department is only paying subsidy for the next twelve months and that they don’t have to pay it again next year, should they decide so. These decisions are based on the local office’s approval of an NGO’s operation. The contract can end if there is non-compliance to technical points, significant or insignificant it may be, to the work of the NGO. These include for example, zoning rights. If an NGO has been helping vulnerable people in a residential setup without the correct zoning, funding will be retracted and people who receive help must get it elsewhere. A PREVAILING PROBLEM Two years ago, we reported on the lack of facilities in the province. There are not enough orphanages, youth care centers, places of safety or shelters in Gauteng. To top that, the department doesn’t employ enough social workers to deal with the magnitude of cases the province faces. And there are already thousands of cases unattended because underfunded NGOs cannot do all the work. If they are closed down due to disappearing financial support, how will the state manage without them and where will the subsidies go? But for now, they wait, in angst for the department’s next move that may leave them in the cold. Although the department signed renewed contracts with NGOs, they have not seen a cent of the money. The standing arrangement was that contracts were signed in April and money was paid out during May. But the department caused its own administrative nightmare, and it doesn’t seem that it has the capacity to rectify a problem it caused for itself. This directly affects the most vulnerable in society. And while there may be many political decisions that led to this mess, Ya Bana’s owners must hustle for money to feed 50 little mouths. All extramural lessons, keeping these kids motivated, must be canceled. 46 of the children placed here, were sent by the Gauteng department of social development itself. It expects the services but does not want to pay for it. MONEY WELL SPENT? Amidst all the turmoil the department caused in the sector, various questions are being raised about how the department chooses to spend its money. Two weeks ago, Gauteng premier Panyaza Lesufi and the MEC of social development, Mbali Hlope announced the Cleaner Greener Gauteng project. Under Lesufi the department of social development was merged with the department of agriculture. It is not clear what the reasoning was behind the merge. The cleaner greener project of the new combined department now employs 6000 people to clean streets and maintain community vegetable gardens. Is this a sustainable solution for poverty relief and job creation in the region at the expense of institutions like Ya Bana that is already making a massive difference? Or is politics in the light of next years’ election the real reason behind local governments’ questionable management of money allocated for vulnerable citizens? SHORT CASE STUDY FOR REFERANCE: The West Rand center for people with disabilities sold its two most crucial assets, its seven-seater van, and its 20-seater bus. These vehicles are used by underpaid care workers who make daily trips to care for bed ridden quadruples, across the West Rand. Other NGOs closed their doors and numerous social workers were retrenched across the board. How can a local government be so detached from the realities faced by the very people they are supposed to serve? The April announcement has resulted in tell-tale signs of the eventual collapse of the entire social welfare system. YA BANA’S STORY Ya Bana has still not received its renewed contract. In fact, the orphanage is still waiting for last years’ subsidy. And before that, it has been waiting since 2017 for the Tshwane metro to approve plans to build the orphanage. Despite this, the department approved and registered Ya Bana. Now, there seems to be a sudden turnaround. In 2014, the department issued a certificate, which allowed Ya Bana to care for 30 children. In 2017, it registered the home to care for 60 kids and the department itself started to place children in Ya Bana’s care. Last year the department renewed the registration, and a contract was signed. To date, not a cent has been paid out. The disclaimer in the new contract now allows the department to negate it obligation to Ya bana, on the basis of the fact that the land is zoned for agriculture. The owners write to DSD every single day but there is no one responding on the other side. They have gone so far as to write to the deputy general director, Onkemetse Kabasia, who played a central role in the budget scandal. But to date, Ya Bana has received no response from either the department or the metro. Meanwhile, a land grab on Ya Bana’s land is well underway. Four of the village’s eight hectares have been taken up by illegal shack dwellers. The children now share the land with loads of people from outside, compromising their safety. Government is doing nothing to stop the land grabs, but Ya Bana is told, they are illegally operating a house for vulnerable children.
